definition: Enactive interfaces are interactive systems that allow organization and transmission of knowledge obtained through action.
details: Examples are interfaces that couple a human with a machine to do things usually done unaided, such as shaping a three-dimensional object using multiple modality interactions with a database, or using interactive video to allow a student to visually engage with mathematical concepts. Enactive interface design can be approached through the idea of raising awareness of affordances, that is, optimization of the awareness of possible actions available to someone using the enactive interface. This optimization involves visibility, affordance, and feedback. The enactive interface in the figure interprets manual input and provides a response in perceptual terms in the form of images, sounds, and haptic (tactile) feedback. The system is called enactive because of the feedback loop in which the system response is decided by the user input, and the user input is driven by the perceived system responses. Enactive interfaces are new types of human-computer interface that express and transmit the enactive knowledge by integrating different sensory aspects. explainer.lead: Enactive interfaces help people learn and build knowledge by doing something, seeing or feeling the result, and adjusting their next action. They matter because some understanding is easier to gain through guided action than through passive reading or watching.

tiers.eli5: Think of learning to shape clay while the clay responds every time you press it. An enactive interface works like that: you act, the computer responds with pictures, sounds, or touch, and those responses guide what you do next.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply the idea by closing a loop between manual input, system interpretation, and perceptual feedback through images, sound, or haptics. Design focuses on visibility, affordances, and feedback so users can recognize available actions; unclear responses or weak feedback can break the action-driven learning loop.
tiers.paperLevel: An enactive interface is an interactive system for organizing and transmitting knowledge acquired through motor action. Its defining loop is user input -> system response -> user perception -> revised user input, with responses expressed through modalities such as images, sounds, and haptic feedback. The central design problem is optimizing awareness of affordances—the actions available to the user—rather than treating action as merely a way to issue commands.

explainer.example: A designer shapes a three-dimensional object through manual input and multimodal interactions with a database. The interface presents the changing result through perceptual feedback, and the designer uses what they see, hear, or feel to decide how to adjust the object next.

usedIn.name: Mathematics education
usedIn.detail: Interactive video lets a student visually engage with mathematical concepts through an action-and-response process.

explainer.intuition: People can acquire knowledge through action, not only through descriptions. An enactive interface supports this by making every action produce a perceptible response that informs the next action.
howItWorks: The user provides manual input to the interface.
The system interprets that input and determines a response.
The response is presented perceptually as images, sounds, or haptic feedback.
The user perceives the response and chooses a new action.
Repetition of this loop supports knowledge acquisition through action.
explainer.whyItMatters: The approach treats motor action as fundamental to storing and acquiring knowledge. It also gives designers a concrete focus: make possible actions visible and provide feedback that helps users understand the effects of their actions.
misconceptions: It is not simply any interface with several sensory modalities; the action-response feedback loop is essential.
Multimodal output alone does not make a system enactive; user input must be driven by perceived system responses.
Affordance awareness is not just about adding controls, but about making available actions and their effects understandable.
